newsitem.title: UK: Sotheby's - an Old Master stained by smuggling.
newsitem.headline: Sotheby's - an Old Master stained by smuggling.

text.p: Like ink spilt on an Old Master, the smuggling scandal that hit Sotheby's on Thursday could badly stain the revered auction house as London battles New York for supremacy of the art world, experts believe.
"This can only do harm. Definitely, without question, sales could be lost because of this," said a former Sotheby's employee on condition of anonymity.
"So much of international trade relies on their supposedly good name that senior management at rival houses can only be greeting this with glee."
Said another industry insider: "This is a potential nightmare. There is so much business to do in a straightforward manner, why engage in smuggling?
"Stolen goods might be worth a great deal of money but it's just not worth our reputation to sell them," he said. "It's mind-boggling that anyone would engage in such activity."
Sotheby's European arm admitted on Thursday that the law had been broken and it suspended senior staff after a television report that it had smuggled art treasures from Italy to Britain.

The programme, to be aired later on Thursday, is expected to show evidence of Sotheby's Old Masters expert in Milan offering to smuggle a Giusseppe Nogari painting to Britain and apparently admitting it was illegal for the portrait to leave Italy. A Sotheby's employee in London is filmed being given the painting.

"The law has been broken in this isolated case," George Bailey, managing director of Sotheby's Europe, told Reuters. "I am very sad about this. We have taken the appropriate action and are also keeping the show on the road."
Nobody doubts that Sotheby's will keep its show on the road but it might be harder for it to nose ahead of the pack in a business renowned for big money and even bigger rivalries.

Founded in London in 1744, Sotheby's is the oldest and among the biggest auctioneers in the world. It employs 1,600 people and has offices in London, New York, Madrid, Rome and Geneva. It has been U.S.-owned since 1983.
Alongside sits Christie's, a fine-art auctioneer established in 1766 that began dabbling in chamber pots and sedan chairs and ended up dealing in Van Goghs and millions.
The two long-established London houses enjoy a keen rivalry but can band together when competing with upstart New York in a market worth some four billion dollars a year.

Despite New York's edge, London is still considered the market with most expertise in key areas such as Old Masters and has the cachet to persuade Europe's old families to part with treasures that don't even exist in the United States.
Dodgy dealing across Europe does not enhance such clout.
"What makes Christie's and Sotheby's different from other auction houses is reputation and integrity and it's crazy that anyone should threaten it," said a senior industry source.
What is more, he said, the art world has cleaned up its act in the past decade, so the scandal was even more of a blow.
"You only have to look at the Elgin Marbles: that was pillage on a grand scale. Things have got a lot cleaner."
But if perception is all in the art world, how will the scandal affect London's bid to catch up with the New York scene?

"Sotheby's are handling it very well but it's terribly sad that this sort of publicity should hit the London market at a time when it is fighting the great fight against the predominance of New York," Neil Smith, secretary of the British Art Market Federation, told Reuters.
"Sotheby's and Christie's bring to this country an enormous amount of business and it's vital this continue. There has been a slip but I have every hope it won't grow into anything wider."
